name: Karst folk
one_line: The streams vanish into the rock, so the water is in the cave and the cistern; the walls are the stones cleared from the field; and the rock itself, burnt, is plaster, mortar and the lime that turns maize into a staple.

needs: geology rock == karst and a cave or sinkhole within 200 m
a cenote, cave pool or resurgence for water, or rain enough to fill a cistern

staples: maize from the milpa, soaked in limewater, with beans and squash between
nuts and figs from the trees that grow on old walls
goat and sheep where the country is dry; snails, game and honey at the sinkhole mouth
how: the milpa: a patch of thin soil between the rocks, cleared, burned, planted, rested
the sinkhole garden: the lush ring at a cenote mouth; walled plots on the dolina floor where the soil collects
goats on the rock pasture, uphill in winter; snaring and gathering at the cave mouth
preserve: maize dried on the cob and kept in the dry cave; nuts in a plastered pit
cheese and meat hung in the cold draught of the cave

fuel.note: branch and brush off the thin woods; hardwood where the dressing biome grows it; the kiln eats brush by the cartload, so kiln and hearth compete for one hillside. Caves are cold but dry: a small fire goes far

shelter.form: a cave mouth walled across with dry stone; round corbelled stone huts out in the fields; every plot walled, every path a lane between walls

TROPICAL_DRY_FOREST.fuel: branch and brush; hardwood is scarce and the kiln wants it
TROPICAL_DRY_FOREST.food: maize, beans and squash on the milpa; ramón nuts; honey; the cenote is the well
TROPICAL_DRY_FOREST.shelter: a plastered stone hut with a thatch roof; the cenote at the centre, steps cut into it
TROPICAL_DRY_FOREST.palette: lime white, dry-forest grey-green, cenote turquoise

MEDITERRANEAN_SCRUB.food: sheep and goats on the rock, wheat in the walled fields, figs and vines on the terraces, cheese
MEDITERRANEAN_SCRUB.shelter: a corbelled stone field hut, slab roofs weighted against the wind, the cistern under the yard
MEDITERRANEAN_SCRUB.palette: pale grey stone, terra rossa red, juniper green

TEMPERATE_DECIDUOUS.fuel: hardwood and branch: the one karst with wood to spare
TEMPERATE_DECIDUOUS.food: maize and beans in the valley, walnuts and chestnuts, hogs on the mast, cheese cooled in the cave
TEMPERATE_DECIDUOUS.shelter: the cave mouth walled, a stone hut beside a sinkhole pond
TEMPERATE_DECIDUOUS.palette: grey limestone, oak green, leaf brown, soot

JUNGLE.food: rice on the flat dolina floor between the towers, taro, fish from the resurgence
JUNGLE.shelter: a house of bamboo and thatch on a stone footing on the dolina floor; the cave is the store
JUNGLE.palette: tower-karst grey, paddy green, mist white

SAVANNA.fuel: brush and dry branch; dung when a herd comes
SAVANNA.food: millet on the dolina floor, goats on the rock, game at the sinkhole pool
SAVANNA.shelter: a stone-walled yard at the cave mouth, thatch on a stone footing
SAVANNA.palette: buff grass, grey pinnacle rock, red earth

knows: maize, beans and squash: the milpa's three, and why the maize wants lime; ramón (breadnut), the tree that grows on old walls and feeds a hungry year
elder, nettle and mallow: the lime-lovers that mark a kiln site or a wall
hart's-tongue fern and moss in the cool of a crack or a cave mouth; wild thyme, sage and juniper on the rock pasture
which cave pool is sweet and which stands stale
plantkeeper.teaches_flavour: why a sinkhole grows tall and green in dry country; why the plants on a kiln ring are the plants on a coast midden (lime)
plantkeeper.teaches_practical: nixtamal: maize soaked in limewater, or it starves you slowly; which plants say there is water under the rock

wants_from_player: brush and wood for the kiln

techniques.name: Cave water
techniques.verb: the water is all underground: follow the cool draught at a cave mouth to the pool, or the vanishing stream to where it comes up again
techniques.teaches: the karst's first lesson, and why the headman gives this one: nothing here works until you know where the water went; it is also the one the player carries out of the karst, since every cave and sinkhole after this is a drink
techniques.unlocks: cave pools, cenotes and resurgences count as drinking water for the player and the camp

techniques.name: The lined spring
techniques.verb: line the resurgence or the seep with fitted stone so it stays clean and does not silt
techniques.teaches: where the water comes back up is the one fixed thing on the hillside; every path leads to it
techniques.unlocks: a clean spring the camp returns to; a lined spring in the bramble is a ruin

techniques.name: The cistern
techniques.verb: cut a bottle-shaped hole in the soft rock, plaster it with lime, apron the mouth so the rain runs in
techniques.teaches: where there is no cenote the rain is the only water, and the rock will not hold it; the plastered hole is the karst's water ceiling
techniques.unlocks: a camp with no cenote holds through the dry season; the ceiling rises above a handful; a dry cistern keeps nuts and grain

techniques.name: Lime
techniques.verb: stack limestone over a pit of brush and branch, burn it a day and a night, slake the white lumps with water
techniques.teaches: the rock is the material: burnt, it is plaster, mortar, whitewash and the limewater that makes maize a staple; and the kiln eats a hillside of brush, the karst's restraint line
techniques.unlocks: plaster, mortar, whitewash; the cistern's lining; the lime for nixtamal

techniques.name: Nixtamal
techniques.verb: soak maize in limewater (or wood-ash lye) overnight, rinse, hull, grind
techniques.teaches: maize alone starves people slowly; soaked in lime it gives up its niacin, and that is why one grain could feed a civilisation
techniques.unlocks: maize counts as a full staple for the player and the camp; without it maize is half a meal

techniques.name: Dry-stone walling
techniques.verb: clear the field of stone and fit the stone into a wall without mortar; corbel it inward and it is a hut
techniques.teaches: the wall is the field's waste made useful; it stands five hundred years and is the ruin
techniques.unlocks: walled plots, terraces on the slope, a round field hut; ridges under the moss when they fall

techniques.name: Cane torch
techniques.verb: bind dry cane, reed or bamboo in a bundle and light one end
techniques.teaches: a cave is entered by torch and left before it burns down; the charred end marks the wall on the way in
techniques.unlocks: a bright, fast-burning torch from reeds or bamboo; its charred stub marks rock: the karst folk's waymark inside a cave

wants: brush and wood for the kiln

ladder: fire at the cave mouth, water from the pool
the milpa on the thin soil; the walls begin as the field is cleared of stone
the cistern and the dry cave: water and grain keep
lime and plaster go out on the road; salt and pots come back
growth.restraint: the milpa is rested and the scrub let back; the kiln burns brush and branch, never the hardwood the hearth needs, and only when the walls need mortar; the rock pasture is grazed in winter and left in summer; the cistern takes only the rain
growth.ceiling_hint: a cenote or a cave stream and soil enough for a milpa reaches the village ceiling; dry karst with no cenote is a foraging handful that lives from the cistern and moves when it runs dry

signatures.what: a net of dry-stone walls across a hillside, lanes between them, the cleared field stones in cairns; ridges under the moss where they fell
signatures.restore: restored: the camp rebuilds the walls on the old footings
signatures.inherits: walled plots and pasture from the first season

signatures.what: a hole with a plastered lip in the rock, a bottle underneath, full of leaves
signatures.restore: restored: dug out and replastered by the lime-burner
signatures.inherits: water through the first dry season

signatures.what: a ring of burnt stone and a white scatter where only lime-lovers grow
signatures.restore: cleared: the pit is dug out and fired again
signatures.inherits: the pit is dug; the first burn is half the work

signatures.what: a sinkhole with steps worn into the rock and a shrine ledge above the water
signatures.restore: restored: fallen brush cleared, the steps re-cut
signatures.inherits: water and the shrine from day one

signatures.what: a cave with a soot-black ceiling, a metre of ash and pot sherds inside the mouth, the wall across it fallen to a ridge
signatures.restore: restored: the wall across the mouth rebuilt, the hearth relit on the old ash
signatures.inherits: a dry shelter and a cold store from the first night

ruin.plants_differ: lime-lovers on the kiln ring and along the walls (elder, nettle, mallow, wild thyme in the cracks) where the hillside grows scrub; a ring of tall lush green at a cenote mouth in dry country; ferns and moss in the cool of the cave mouth

aesthetic.silhouette: grey walls netting a hillside; a round corbelled hut like a beehive; a black cave mouth walled halfway; a white plastered house; a sinkhole ringed with green
sounds: a stream going quiet into the rock
goat bells on rock; the kiln roaring; swifts at a sinkhole mouth
props: the plastered cistern mouth and the lime kiln ring
worn steps into a cenote; a cane torch stub

huts.workshop_form: a round corbelled stone hut, lime-whitewashed, a thatch-and-brush cap and a doorway wide enough to work in the light; it stands beside the kiln ring
soft: a goat hide pegged on a frame, a stone scraper beside it
cane and reed split and soaking in a trough, a half-woven basket
maize husk and bark fibre twisted into cord on a hank
a thatch bundle being tied, poles and brush racked behind
hard: a floor of limestone chips and a half-dressed wall stone
a bone awl and goat horn on a slab, a stone mallet
a quern slab with a maize cob mid-grind, a mano on it
a bucket of slaked lime and a plastering trowel of wood
hearth: a nixtamal pot of maize steeping in limewater
a goat stew pot on three stones
a bundle of cane torches stood up to dry beside the fire
kiln: the lime kiln: a ring of burnt stone with limestone stacked over a brush pit
a white heap of slaked lime and pots drying on a rock shelf
the clay pit, wet and red, cut into a pocket of terra rossa
huts.porch_sign: a white-plastered doorway with a handprint in lime and a bundle of cane torches leaning by it
huts.library: a dry cave recess walled across with fitted stone, a plastered floor and shelf; the winter-count is painted in pictures on a smooth whitewashed wall panel, with a string of knots hung beside it
third_places: the cenote steps at dusk, swifts overhead

real_world.analogue: Maya of the Yucatán (a living people): cenotes and chultuns
real_world.region: Yucatán Peninsula, Mexico; the Puuc hills
real_world.note: a limestone peninsula with almost no rivers: the cenotes (Yucatec ts'onot, a sinkhole open on the water table) were the only perennial drinking water, cities such as Chichén Itzá were built around them, and they were sacred, the home of the rain god Chaac and a door to the underworld, given offerings; in the Puuc hills, far above the aquifer, bottle-shaped chultuns cut in the rock with a plastered apron caught the rain instead, and elsewhere stored ramón nuts

real_world.region: Mesoamerica, earliest evidence on Guatemala's Pacific coast c. 1500–1200 BCE
real_world.note: maize soaked and cooked in limewater or wood-ash lye: it softens the hull, frees the niacin and adds calcium; where maize spread without the process (northern Italy, the US South) pellagra followed

real_world.region: Puuc region, northern Yucatán, c. 650–850 CE
real_world.note: annular pit-kilns burned limestone at 800 °C and more into quicklime for plaster, mortar and stucco; the kilns needed less wood than open burning, which mattered in a fuel-scarce landscape, and nearly half the household groups had their own

real_world.analogue: The Dinaric karst: the Kras of Slovenia and Istria
real_world.note: the Kras plateau gave karst its name; the Reka sinks into the Škocjan caves; villages drank from clay-lined ponds (kali) and rain cisterns (štirne) because the rock holds nothing; fields were cleared stone by stone into dry-stone walls, and in Istria into round corbelled kažun field huts (most 18th–19th c.); dry-stone walling is UNESCO intangible heritage (2018)

real_world.analogue: Guangxi karst farmers (Zhuang, Han and others)
real_world.region: Guilin and Yangshuo, South China Karst
real_world.note: rice on the flat valley and dolina floors between limestone towers (fenglin) and peak clusters (fengcong); the soil on the slopes is thin and goes to bare rock when stripped; the water drains underground; a World Heritage karst since 2007

real_world.region: Kentucky, USA; Early Woodland c. 1000–200 BCE
real_world.note: people went more than 19 miles into the cave by the light of river-cane torches to mine gypsum and mirabilite from the walls, leaving cane baskets, gourds, woven slippers and drawings made with charred torch tips; saltpetre for gunpowder was dug there much later (1812), a note only
